title: Database Bottlenecks
subtitle: Diagnosing and resolving CPU saturation, Disk IOPS exhaustion, Lock Contention, N+1 queries, and MVCC bloat.
keyTakeaways: Database performance issues usually originate from one of four physical bottlenecks: CPU saturation, Disk IOPS exhaustion, Lock Contention, or Memory Buffer Thrashing.
The N+1 query antipattern saturates database connection pools and network bandwidth by issuing hundreds of individual queries inside application loops.
PostgreSQL MVCC table bloat and Transaction ID (XID) wraparound freeze occur when autovacuum cannot keep up with high write rates or long-running transactions.

sections.heading: Query-Level Bottlenecks: N+1 Storms and Missing Indexes
sections.body: Most database performance crises start in application code rather than the database engine itself. ORM abstractions make it deceptively easy to introduce severe query amplification.
bullets: The N+1 Query Antipattern: Fetching 50 orders and then looping through each order to query its user (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = order.user_id`) issues 51 sequential queries. Each query pays network RTT and connection overhead. Solved by eager loading (`JOIN` or `WHERE id IN (...)`).
Missing Composite Indexes: Queries sorting and filtering on multiple columns execute full sequential scans or temporary disk sorts when missing matching composite indexes.
Deep Offset Pagination: `OFFSET 100000` forces the database to scan and discard 100,000 index entries, burning CPU and disk IOPS.

sections.heading: Storage Engine Bottlenecks: MVCC Bloat and Lock Contention
sections.body: Even with optimized queries, storage engines hit operational bottlenecks under heavy continuous write load.
bullets: Postgres MVCC Bloat: When rows update frequently, dead row versions accumulate. If a long-running transaction or forgotten analytics query stays open for hours, Postgres cannot vacuum dead rows newer than that transaction's snapshot. Tables balloon in size, degrading cache efficiency.

Transaction ID (XID) Wraparound: Postgres uses 32-bit transaction IDs (capping at ~2 billion transactions). If autovacuum cannot freeze old transaction IDs before reaching the limit, Postgres forcibly enters emergency read-only mode to prevent silent data corruption.

Hot-Row Lock Contention: If 500 concurrent threads execute `SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE`, they queue behind a single row lock. Throughput drops to the serial execution speed of a single core.

tradeOffs.pros: Fetches all related data in a single network round trip; database engine optimizes join execution plan.
tradeOffs.cons: Multiplies row volume over the wire if relations are one-to-many (cartesian product bloat).

tradeOffs.pros: Prevents cartesian product bloat; clean separation of queries; easy to cache individual entity queries.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires two network round trips; application must stitch relations in memory.
tradeOffs.bestFor: GraphQL resolvers and deep microservice domain models.

interviewTip: When asked how to diagnose a slow database in production, outline a systematic debugging sequence: 'First, inspect database metrics to identify the physical bottleneck: CPU, Disk IOPS, Memory, or Connection Pool saturation. Second, query `pg_stat_statements` to find queries with the highest total execution time. Third, check `pg_stat_activity` for long-running transactions blocking autovacuum or holding exclusive row locks.'
